items.questionAndWhy: How does a preceding sentence change the neural representation of a word as natural language unfolds? Understanding contextual meaning is important because identical words can convey different information depending on what came before them.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers analyzed single-neuron recordings from the human hippocampus in ten participants while they listened to podcasts. They compared neural responses with lexical-semantic representations, word position within clauses and weighted embeddings of preceding words, including attention weights from a large language model.
items.whatTheyFound: Hippocampal neurons encoded clause-relative word position, including ordinal and frequency-domain patterns. Word responses reflected both the word's lexical meaning and preceding context; relative contextual weighting correlated with LLM attention weights. This is correlational neural decoding in a small intracranial-recording sample, not proof that human language comprehension executes a transformer algorithm.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX narrative and sensemaking studies should distinguish the meaning of isolated terms from context-conditioned interpretation. It is reasonable to test whether sequence and prior context change message comprehension, but neural resemblance to LLM attention does not validate a particular influence mechanism or an LLM as a cognitive model.
items.streamTitle: Hippocampal neurons represented word meaning in the context of preceding language
items.streamSummary: Single-neuron recordings from ten podcast listeners linked hippocampal responses to word position and weighted preceding semantic context. Neural weights correlated with LLM attention patterns, but algorithmic equivalence and message effects were not demonstrated.
items.attribution: Katlowitz et al. — Nature Human Behaviour (human intracranial language study; November 23, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Does prolonged physical effort reduce a person's ability to perform cognitive tasks, or instead reduce their willingness to invest further cognitive and physical effort? These are different explanations for apparent fatigue.
items.whatTheyDid: Two within-subject crossover experiments (n=30 and n=32) compared 50–60 minutes of moderately hard versus extremely light cycling. Participants completed sustained-attention and other cognitive tasks during cycling, then made reward-versus-effort choices. The second experiment used incentive-compatible choices, and the authors fitted effort-discounting models.
items.whatTheyFound: After harder cycling, participants discounted rewards requiring additional cognitive and physical effort more steeply, while measured cognitive performance remained largely unchanged. Modeling suggested a lower effort-acceptance threshold, and heart-rate indicators related to the shift. These short-duration controlled experiments do not establish how prolonged field operations affect cognition.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX decision and training studies, measure capacity to perform a task separately from willingness to undertake it. An analyst can retain accuracy while becoming less inclined to invest effort. Transfer to operational stress or extended work shifts requires targeted replication, not direct substitution of cycling effects.
items.streamTitle: Physical exertion reduced willingness to expend cognitive effort without impairing measured performance
items.streamSummary: In two crossover cycling experiments (30 and 32 participants), more strenuous exercise increased discounting of rewards requiring later mental or physical effort while cognitive-task performance was largely unchanged. The result distinguishes motivation from capacity.
items.attribution: Massar, Sasmita, Obana et al. — Scientific Reports (two within-subject crossover experiments; November 23, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do online students engage more when webcams are on, and does the answer depend on whether camera participation is symmetrical and how strongly learners compare themselves with peers?
items.whatTheyDid: A research program with Taiwanese university English-language learners combined a 321-person survey of four visibility configurations, an EEG experiment (n=40), a mediation test (n=40), and a 16-week within-subject field experiment (n=32) examining social-comparison orientation.
items.whatTheyFound: Symmetric all-on and all-off settings yielded similarly high self-reported motivation, while asymmetric visibility produced lower motivation. Camera use increased neurophysiological engagement in an experimental comparison, but social facilitation did not statistically mediate the proposed effect. High social-comparison participants showed more adverse effects of visibility; lower-comparison participants were comparatively unaffected. Different samples and outcome types limit a simple general policy claim.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX remote practitioner courses and collaborative exercises could evaluate equitable visibility arrangements and individual differences, rather than mandating camera-on participation as a universal engagement tool. The Taiwan EFL setting does not establish results for multinational operational teams.
items.streamTitle: Webcam asymmetry and social-comparison orientation shaped online learning engagement
items.streamSummary: Four studies of Taiwanese university learners found comparable motivation with all cameras on or all off, lower motivation in asymmetric conditions, and stronger negative visibility effects among high social-comparison learners. Proposed social-facilitation mediation was not supported.
items.attribution: Liwei Hsu and Yi Hsu — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (survey, EEG, mediation and field studies; November 23, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do known manipulation networks and the infrastructure supporting them persist across electoral contexts despite identification, exposure and takedown efforts? How should analysts separate campaign activity from effects on real audiences?
items.whatTheyDid: Alliance4Europe published a November synthesis of its and Counter Disinformation Network members' January–November 2026 investigations. It traced account networks across elections, examples of Matryoshka and Doppelganger operations, AI-produced content, advertising and platform enforcement, explicitly distinguishing data claims from analysis.
items.whatTheyFound: The report documents an X network shifting between national elections, including 8,505 accounts identified in a Swedish context, and says fewer than 1% of previously logged accounts had been removed as far as investigators could assess. It also reports heterogeneous platform responses and repeat use of exposed infrastructure. These figures combine several investigations with differing methods; observed activity and removal rates do not quantify persuasion, voter impact or independently establish every operator attribution.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX OIE assessment, maintain persistent infrastructure identities across campaigns and measure enforcement, authentic reach and audience response separately. An observed network moving across campaigns supports continuity analysis; it does not establish the success of any political influence objective.
items.streamTitle: European manipulation report documented recurring networks and uneven platform enforcement
items.streamSummary: Alliance4Europe's November synthesis traced repeated account and infrastructure use across elections and reported uneven platform enforcement, including an 8,505-account Swedish network. These are investigative activity measures, not demonstrated voter-persuasion effects.
items.attribution: Alliance4Europe / Counter Disinformation Network — State of Manipulation: A Threat to Europe's Security (investigative synthesis; November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do AI assistants support a person's ability to make and understand decisions, rather than merely supplying compliant answers? How can this be assessed as several distinct behaviors?
items.whatTheyDid: HumanAgencyBench, a peer-reviewed NLP benchmark, operationalized six dimensions: asking clarifying questions, avoiding value manipulation, correcting misinformation, deferring important decisions, encouraging learning and maintaining social boundaries. The authors used LLM-assisted generation and validation of test queries and evaluation of assistant responses across multiple systems.
items.whatTheyFound: Evaluated assistants provided low-to-moderate support for agency, with substantial differences across systems and dimensions. Strength in one dimension did not guarantee strength in another, and increased general model capability did not consistently improve agency support. Because scoring relies partly on AI-assisted judgments and constructed prompts, it does not directly measure users' later independent decisions.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX AI-supported research and education should test whether tools help users preserve decision authority, correct unsupported assumptions and learn independently. Treat agency as multidimensional and supplement benchmark scores with actual human-user outcomes before claims of improved judgment.
items.streamTitle: HumanAgencyBench separated six dimensions of AI support for user agency
items.streamSummary: A peer-reviewed benchmark found variable and generally limited assistant support across clarification, misinformation correction, value autonomy, important decisions, learning and boundaries. Simulated evaluation scores do not establish changes in human agency.
items.attribution: Sturgeon, Samuelson, Haimes and Anthis — Findings of EMNLP 2026 (peer-reviewed AI-assistant evaluation; October 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can communication among AI agents cause new stereotypical judgments or amplify existing ones, even when each model is evaluated individually?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers introduced separate metrics for emergence, propagation and amplification of stereotypical bias in multi-agent LLM systems. They evaluated three bias benchmarks while varying model backbones, social-group configurations, interaction patterns and adversarial prompts.
items.whatTheyFound: In the tested settings, communication produced up to 70% newly emerging bias, spread biased outputs to more than 80% of agents and amplified stereotype signals by over threefold. Denser and competitive interaction often increased the problem, while tested defenses provided limited protection. These are benchmark-specific AI-agent output metrics; no human participants or human stereotype adoption were evaluated.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX multi-agent research workflows, checking each agent in isolation is inadequate if later conversations can amplify unsupported judgments. Test group interactions and adversarial contamination explicitly; do not interpret LLM bias propagation as empirical evidence of human social contagion.
items.streamTitle: Multi-agent conversations amplified stereotypical bias in benchmark simulations
items.streamSummary: Across three bias benchmarks, communication among LLM agents sometimes generated new biased outputs, propagated them broadly and magnified stereotype metrics more than threefold. This is simulated AI-system behavior, not evidence of human-group effects.
items.attribution: Nguyen, Luo, Kaur et al. — Findings of IJCNLP-AACL 2026 (peer-reviewed multi-agent benchmark; November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can analysts distinguish coordinated inauthentic social-media accounts from users who merely respond simultaneously to the same trending event? Can detection adapt across campaigns without intensive repeated manual labeling?
items.whatTheyDid: ACCD combines context-indexed reuse of convergent-cross-mapping settings, active learning for uncertain account pairs and later estimator-based verification. Researchers evaluated pair-level coordination detection on the Twitter Internet Research Agency dataset, Reddit traces and synthetic networks with known causal structures.
items.whatTheyFound: On the IRA benchmark, pair-level F1 increased from 75.8% to 87.3% against a fixed-parameter causal baseline, with 68.3% less manual labeling and 2.5-times faster end-to-end detection. Reddit F1 was 84.7%; synthetic influence-edge AUROC reached 0.934 versus 0.708 for correlation screening. These are benchmark estimates; inferred time-series causal edges are not independently established operator direction or behavioral influence in the field.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX information-environment analysis, ACCD offers a candidate screening workflow to prioritize account pairs and preserve uncertainty before analyst attribution. Evaluate it prospectively on known-ground-truth operations and separate coordination detection from influence effects or responsibility assignment.
items.streamTitle: Adaptive causal coordination screening improved detection of inauthentic account pairs
items.streamSummary: ACCD raised pair-level F1 from 75.8% to 87.3% on an IRA benchmark while reducing labeling and runtime; synthetic tests also improved influence-edge recovery. Such screening does not verify real-world causality, operator attribution or persuasion.
items.attribution: Han, Ding, Chen and Tao — NLP4PI workshop, ACL Anthology (peer-reviewed detection-method evaluation; October 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can researchers compare how different language communities describe the same event under narrative versus formal reporting goals, rather than comparing unrelated naturally occurring texts or translations?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers released a standardized online elicitation dataset from 1,200 participants: 100 native speakers in each of 12 languages, each writing two descriptions of common event scenarios, one narrative to a friend and one expository to an authority. The resulting 2,400 texts and reusable task materials are available openly.
items.whatTheyFound: The dataset enables controlled comparison of language, scenario and audience/genre framing. The authors report similar text lengths across conditions and illustrative register differences, such as more formal salutations in expository texts. It is a data descriptor, not a measured finding that one genre is more persuasive; the genre manipulation also changed the addressee, and the language sample is not globally representative.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX cross-cultural narrative research can use the corpus to benchmark event-description coding and test whether an analytic system confuses linguistic or addressee differences with changed underlying events. Any inference about actual comprehension, belief change or influence effectiveness requires new human-outcome evidence.
items.streamTitle: Twelve-language corpus enables controlled comparison of narrative and formal event descriptions
items.streamSummary: An open dataset contains 2,400 accounts of shared events from 1,200 people across 12 languages and two discourse settings. It supports cross-linguistic event-framing research, not conclusions about message persuasiveness.
items.attribution: Peeters, Kamakura, Gonçalves et al. — Scientific Data (public multilingual text dataset; November 23, 2026)
